strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practical problem (efficient, data-light GUI grounding) with a novel angle: rather than adding embedding-based grounding modules (as GUI-Actor does) or generating text coordinates, it directly supervises the model's intrinsic multi-head self-attention, which is architecturally simpler and avoids extra warm-up training.

The technical contributions are reasonably well-motivated and incrementally justified: the <ANCHOR> token to avoid per-query-token aggregation, the visual-sink query token selection based on hidden-state similarity (rather than raw attention) to identify semantic heads, and the overlap/center-aware patch-wise labeling scheme. The rationale for using hidden-state similarity instead of attention magnitude to select visual-sink tokens is supported by an appendix analysis (Fig. 5) showing attention-based selection can pick semantically irrelevant tokens.

Strong empirical results: GUI-AIMA-3B achieves state-of-the-art performance among 3B-scale models on ScreenSpot-Pro and OSWorld-G, and is competitive with much larger 7B/72B models, using only ~85k training images / 259k instructions — substantially less data than many SFT baselines trained on millions of examples.

Thorough ablation studies isolate the contribution of each design choice (vanilla vs. simplified attention grounding vs. GUI-Actor, attention head weighting variants, Qs selection strategies, patch-wise labeling), and convergence plots (Fig. 4) support the claimed training efficiency and stability advantages over vanilla attention grounding and GUI-Actor.

The zoom-in inference analysis (Table 5, Section 4.3) provides a useful breakdown of how much of the accuracy gain comes from cropping alone vs. actual zoom, and examines the recovered/lost trade-off at different zoom factors, adding evidential rigor beyond a single aggregate number.
The paper is generally clear in exposition, with helpful figures (Fig. 2, Fig. 3) illustrating the vanilla vs. simplified attention aggregation and the three-step weighting pipeline.
weaknesses: The method is only validated on a single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-3B); it is unclear whether the attention-based approach and the specific head-weighting mechanism generalize to other MLLM architectures/backbones (e.g., different attention head structures, different vision encoders), which limits claims of general applicability of the 'intrinsic attention' insight.

The two-step zoom-in procedure, while effective, relies on manually tuned hyperparameters (crop size 448px, 2x zoom ratio) chosen via analysis on the test/analysis set (Table 5 shows different zoom factors evaluated on ScreenSpot-Pro itself), raising a mild risk of overfitting these inference-time choices to the benchmark rather than a principled, dataset-agnostic default.

The 'soft' matching variant (Eq. 11) is introduced and shown to sometimes outperform the main variant (e.g., ScreenSpot-Pro Table 1), but the paper doesn't clearly justify which variant should be treated as the primary proposed model, creating some ambiguity in the core contribution and complicating fair comparison/reproducibility.

No confidence intervals, variance across seeds, or statistical significance testing is reported; given some ablation gains are on the order of 1-2%, it's hard to assess whether observed differences (e.g., top-1 vs top-3 Qs, global vs layer-wise) are robust or within noise.

Only 3B and no larger AIMA variant is trained/evaluated, so it remains unclear whether the benefits of attention-based grounding hold or diminish at larger model scales, despite claims of comparability with much larger baselines (7B/72B) which use different training paradigms and are not apples-to-apples controlled comparisons.

The paper's claim that 'light training can trigger native grounding capability' is suggestive but not deeply probed theoretically or via more rigorous mechanistic analysis beyond the qualitative attention visualizations in the appendix; the link between the head-weighting heuristic and true 'semantic head' identification is empirically motivated but not formally validated.

Some baseline comparisons in Tables 1-3 use numbers directly copied from original papers, which may differ in evaluation protocol/hardware/prompt format, introducing potential inconsistencies not fully controlled for in the comparison.

strengths: Introduces a conceptually clean simplification of attention-based GUI grounding via a learnable <ANCHOR> token that implicitly aggregates query-token attentions, avoiding the need for extra grounding modules (in contrast to GUI-Actor) or manual heuristics over all query tokens (in contrast to TAG/vanilla attention grounding).

Proposes a principled attention-head weighting scheme based on 'visual-sink query tokens' identified from hidden-state similarity rather than raw attention values, with a supporting analysis (Appendix A) showing that hidden-state-derived and attention-derived visual correlation patterns diverge, justifying the design choice.

Strong empirical results: GUI-AIMA-3B achieves state-of-the-art performance among 3B models on ScreenSpot-Pro and OSWorld-G, and is competitive with much larger 7B/72B models, while using only ~85k training images—substantially less data than most SFT baselines.

Comprehensive ablation study (Table 4) that isolates the contribution of each component (anchor token, head weighting variants, choice of K and layer-wise vs. global Qs, weighted patch-wise labeling), providing reasonably convincing evidence for each design decision.

The training-free two-step zoom-in inference is a practical, low-cost extension enabled directly by the coordinate-free/patch-wise formulation, and is analyzed in detail (Table 5) showing meaningful reduction of offset errors on high-resolution screenshots.
Convergence analysis (Fig. 4) supports the claim of improved training efficiency and stability relative to vanilla attention grounding and GUI-Actor.
Clear positioning relative to prior coordinate-based and coordinate-free GUI grounding literature, with reasonable coverage of related work.
weaknesses: All experiments use a single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-3B); it remains unclear whether the proposed attention-alignment mechanism, visual-sink token identification, and head-weighting scheme generalize to other MLLM architectures or larger scales, which limits the generality of the claims about 'intrinsic' attention patterns.

Some ablation improvements are numerically small (e.g., global top-1 Qs vs. uniform weighting is ~0.5-1.9% depending on benchmark), and the paper does not report variance across seeds/runs, making it hard to judge statistical robustness of the specific design choices.

The relationship between the 'hard' (Eq. 8, global top-1 Qs) and 'soft' (Eq. 11) variants is inconsistent across benchmarks (soft is better on ScreenSpot-Pro but the hard variant is better on ScreenSpot-v2/OSWorld-G) without a clear explanation or guidance on which to prefer in practice.

The ablation study for coordinate-free modeling comparisons (Table 4) uses a smaller 45k training subset while the main results (Table 1-3) use the full 259k/85k-image dataset, which introduces a slight inconsistency when interpreting how much of the final performance gain is attributable to the core method vs. additional data.
The zoom-in crop size (448 px) and zoom ratio (2x) appear to be manually tuned hyperparameters; while an ablation over zoom factor is provided, sensitivity to crop size itself is not explored.

The attempted extension to multi-region grounding via multiple <ANCHOR> tokens failed to show gains (Appendix C), which is honestly reported but suggests the current architecture may not trivially extend beyond single-target grounding, limiting broader applicability to multi-target agent tasks.
Reproducibility could be strengthened; although a project page is mentioned, no explicit confirmation of code/model release is given in the manuscript text provided.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem (coordinate-free, attention-based GUI grounding) and proposes a technically clean solution: a learnable <ANCHOR> token to avoid impractical token-wise attention aggregation, plus a head-weighting scheme based on visual-sink query tokens identified via hidden-state similarity.

Extensive experiments across five diverse benchmarks (ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2, ScreenSpot-v1, OSWorld-G, UI-Vision, MMBench-GUI-L2) show consistent, strong results at the 3B scale, often competitive with much larger 7B/72B models, and the method achieves state-of-the-art among 3B models.

Data efficiency is a notable and well-supported claim: GUI-AIMA-3B is trained on only ~101k-509k samples yet is competitive with models trained on much larger corpora (e.g., 9.6M for GUI-Actor+Verifier), which is a meaningful practical contribution.

Thorough ablation studies isolate the contribution of each design choice (anchor token vs vanilla attention vs GUI-Actor embeddings; head-weighting strategies; patch labeling scheme; zoom-in ablation with Relax@k analysis), providing good evidence for the necessity of each component.

The two-step zoom-in inference is a simple, training-free extension enabled naturally by the coordinate-free/patch-based formulation, and the paper provides a careful quantitative analysis of when/why it helps (offset correction statistics in Table 6).

Training/inference efficiency analysis (Table 8, attention extraction complexity reduction) and interpretability analysis (head-weight visualization, Fig. 6) add useful practical and mechanistic insight beyond raw accuracy numbers.
weaknesses: The core contributions (anchor token for aggregation, head-weighting) are incremental relative to closely related prior work (TAG's attention grounding, GUI-Actor's <ACTOR> token), and the paper's main novelty is in combining/refining existing ideas rather than a fundamentally new formulation; the paper should more clearly delineate what is conceptually new versus a recombination.

The patch-wise labeling (Eq. 6) is explicitly borrowed from GUI-G^2 (Tang et al., 2025), and the general idea of coordinate-free grounding via attention is from TAG/GUI-Actor, somewhat limiting the perceived originality despite decent engineering.

The visual-sink query token selection method (Eq. 4-5) is motivated by intuition and qualitative evidence (Fig. 4, Fig. 7) rather than a rigorous theoretical justification for why hidden-state similarity is superior to attention-based signals; the explanation relies on citations to other work without a deeper causal analysis specific to this setting.

Ablation studies are conducted on a small 45k subset (and 85k/259k in appendix) rather than the full 509k training set, raising questions about whether conclusions fully transfer to the final model configuration; this is a reasonable computational compromise but somewhat weakens the ablation's direct relevance to the reported SOTA numbers.

Some baseline comparisons are not entirely apples-to-apples (e.g., GUI-AIMA-3B uses additional 250k GroundCUA data not available to some competitors, and UI-Vision is in-domain for GUI-AIMA-3B and GroundNext but not for others), which could inflate perceived advantages if not carefully controlled for in the narrative.

The paper's analysis of why higher weights concentrate in mid-to-late layers (Section 4.5) is largely descriptive/visual rather than offering deeper mechanistic explanation, limiting the depth of understanding gained.

Presentation could be improved: notation is dense (many symbols introduced rapidly), and some figures/tables (e.g., Table 1) are very large and could benefit from clearer summarization or highlighting of the key comparisons for readability.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated technical contribution: reformulating GUI grounding as coordinate-free attention supervision is a sensible alternative to text-based coordinate generation, and the paper clearly differentiates itself from prior attention-based (TAG) and embedding-based (GUI-Actor) approaches.

Strong empirical results across five diverse benchmarks (ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2, OSWorld-G, UI-Vision, MMBench-GUI-L2), achieving SOTA among 3B-scale models and remaining competitive with much larger models trained on far more data.

Excellent data efficiency: GUI-AIMA-3B uses only ~101k screenshots/509k instructions, substantially less than many competing methods (e.g., GUI-Actor uses 9.6M samples), which is a meaningful practical contribution.

Thorough and well-designed ablation studies that isolate the contribution of each proposed component (anchor token vs. vanilla aggregation, head-weighting strategies, visual-sink token selection with varying K, patch-wise labeling), lending good support to the design choices.

The proposed two-step zoom-in inference is simple, requires no additional training, and is shown via a targeted offset-error analysis (Table 6) to meaningfully correct near-miss predictions, particularly for high-resolution desktop scenarios.

Additional analyses (attention head pruning in Section 4.5, convergence curves in Fig. 5, visual-sink token distribution in Fig. 4, appendix similarity analysis) provide good interpretability and mechanistic insight into why the method works.

Efficient attention extraction (eager attention only on grounding-relevant rows) is a practical engineering contribution with reported negligible overhead, and training/inference time comparisons with GUI-Actor are provided.
weaknesses: The method is only validated on a single MLLM backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-3B); it remains unclear how well the anchor-token/attention-supervision approach generalizes to other architectures or larger scales, which limits confidence in the generality of the claims.

The large accuracy jumps reported for the two-step zoom-in stage (e.g., +7.7 points on ScreenSpot-Pro) partially conflate the contribution of the core attention-alignment method with that of the zoom-in inference trick; the paper could more clearly disentangle how much of the state-of-the-art claim rests on each component.

Persistent and substantial text-vs-icon performance gap (e.g., Table 1: 70.0% text vs 47.9% icon even with zoom-in) suggests the method still struggles with icon-based grounding relative to text-based grounding, and this limitation is not deeply analyzed or discussed.

The visual-sink query token selection relies on a heuristic (cosine similarity of hidden states aggregated across layers) that, while empirically justified via ablation, lacks a deeper theoretical grounding for why hidden-state similarity is preferable to attention-based signals in principle.

Comparisons across baselines involve considerably different training data scales and sources (e.g., GroundNext uses more in-domain data, GUI-Actor uses 9.6M samples with a verifier), which the paper is transparent about, but this heterogeneity somewhat complicates apples-to-apples interpretation of the state-of-the-art claims.

Multi-region or ambiguous-instruction grounding scenarios are not evaluated; the paper explicitly defers a multi-anchor extension to future work, so the current method's applicability is confined to single-region grounding.
